items.question: A team's utilization rises from 80% to 90%. By the chapter's curve, what happens to the average wait?
choices: It rises by about an eighth, in line with the extra load
It more than doubles, from about 4 to about 9 times the service time
It stays flat until utilization reaches 100%
It falls, because busier teams finish work faster

explanation.text: The curve turns steep past 80%: the wait goes from about 4 to about 9 times the service time, far faster than the rise in load.

items.question: Two teams run at the same 85% utilization, but one gets requests in unpredictable bursts. Which team waits longer, according to the chapter?
choices: Neither: at equal utilization the waits are equal
The team with steady arrivals, because it never gets a break
The team with bursty arrivals, because variability multiplies the effect of utilization

explanation.text: Waiting scales with utilization and variability together, so at equal load the more variable arrivals produce longer queues.

items.question: Which planning practice does the chapter warn against?
choices: Planning every sprint to 100% of available capacity
Spending slack on interruptions before improvement work
Measuring utilization over several weeks before changing plans

explanation.text: Planning to full capacity leaves unplanned work nowhere to go, so queues are guaranteed; the other three are the chapter's own recommendations.
